summary: b (Select formula and enter parameters) is what the Quadratic formula calculator works out, and it gets there from the C, the K and the discriminant (Δ) (Results (Δ & solutions)). Think of it as a shortcut for a homework check, a spreadsheet build or a bit of mental arithmetic you want to confirm. The formula is printed further down, so you can check the answer by hand if you want to.

sections.title: How does the Quadratic formula calculator work?
sections.html:
The Quadratic formula calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports b (Select formula and enter parameters) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the formula form); then you type in the c (Select formula and enter parameters), the k (Select formula and enter parameters) and the discriminant (Δ) (Results (Δ & solutions)).

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Quadratic formula calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

B=the square root of (4 × A × C + discriminant (Δ))
H=-1 ÷ 2 × B ÷ A
B=2 × the square root of (A × (C − K))
B=-2 × A × X₁,₂ real part
X₁,₂ imaginary part +/-=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (the absolute value of (discriminant (Δ))) ÷ A
X₂=-X₁ − B ÷ A

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Formula form set to Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0, A = 10, C = 10 and Discriminant (Δ) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives B = 20.2485, H = -1.0124, K = -0.25 and x₁ = -1.1705.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: B = 20.2485, H = -1.0124, K = -0.25 and x₁ = -1.1705 should be roughly the size you expected from Formula form set to Ax^2 + Bx + C = 0 and A = 10.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Quadratic formula calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Building the same calculation into a spreadsheet and wanting a reference value
  • Settling an argument about a number with a quick, traceable result
  • Checking a homework answer before you hand it in
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the C, the K and the discriminant (Δ) (Results (Δ & solutions)) — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Quadratic formula calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns b (Select formula and enter parameters), derived from the C, the K and the discriminant (Δ) (Results (Δ & solutions)). Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Quadratic formula calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the C, the K and the discriminant (Δ) (Results (Δ & solutions)), which is 13 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports B = 20.2485. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Quadratic formula calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
